passages.happening:
Moses and Aaron go to Pharaoh and say, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘Let My people go, so that they may hold a feast to Me in the wilderness’” (verse 1).

“But Pharaoh replied, ‘Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and I will not let Israel go’” (verse 2).

They ask again, for three days in the wilderness “to sacrifice to the LORD our God” (verse 3). Pharaoh answers, “Moses and Aaron, why do you draw the people away from their work? Get back to your labor!” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
After the hopeful end of chapter 4, this is the first meeting with Pharaoh. It goes about as badly as it could.

Moses speaks as a messenger: ‘This is what the LORD says’. That was how a king's messenger began. But Pharaoh is a king too, and in his world he was more. Egyptians honored their king as the son of the sun god and the living Horus. Egypt had many gods. The god of a slave people, whose name Pharaoh had never heard, had no claim on him.

‘I do not know the LORD.’ This is the question of the next ten chapters. God's answer will come again and again, in the words ‘so that you may know that I am the LORD’. Pharaoh does not know him yet. He will.

The verb for ‘hold a feast’ is the one Israel later used for its pilgrim feasts, when the people went up three times a year to appear before God. Worship here means going somewhere and offering sacrifice. Chapter 8 will explain why it could not be done inside Egypt.

To Pharaoh it is all a waste of working time. ‘Get back to your labor.’ He reads the wish to worship as laziness.
passages.later:
God answers Pharaoh's question through the whole story. Before the plagues he says, “And the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD, when I stretch out My hand against Egypt and bring the Israelites out from among them” (Exodus 7:5).

The feast in the wilderness becomes Israel's pattern of worship: “Three times a year you are to celebrate a feast to Me” (Exodus 23:14).

Paul quotes God's word to Pharaoh about why he raised him up: “that I might display My power in you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth” (Romans 9:17).
passages.hard:
Was Moses' request for a short trip to worship a deception, since God meant to bring Israel out for good? God told Moses to ask for exactly this (3:18), and God had also said he would bring Israel to Canaan (3:8).

Readers handle this in several ways. Many see a real but modest first request that shows what is in Pharaoh's heart: if he will not give slaves a few days to worship, he will never set them free, and his refusal justifies what follows. Others stress that the request was true as far as it went. The first goal God named was worship at the mountain (3:12), and the break with Egypt becomes complete because Pharaoh makes things worse, not because Moses lied. A third group grants that the request held back the full plan, and compares it with other places where the weak outwit a murderous power, such as the midwives in chapter 1. The text records it without praise or blame.

On every view, Pharaoh's objection was never about the length of the trip. He rejects any claim the LORD has on his slaves, and he answers even the smallest request with a heavier load. These notes take no side on the rest.
passages.asks: Pharaoh asked, ‘Who is the LORD that I should obey?’ Ask whether there is any part of your life where you have asked the same question, out loud or in silence. And ask whether you, like Pharaoh, ever treat time given to God as time wasted.

passages.happening:
That same day Pharaoh orders the taskmasters and foremen: “You shall no longer supply the people with straw for making bricks. They must go and gather their own straw. But require of them the same quota of bricks as before; do not reduce it. For they are lazy” (verses 7-8).

“Make the work harder on the men so they will be occupied and pay no attention to these lies” (verse 9).

So the people scatter all over Egypt to gather stubble for straw (verse 12). The taskmasters keep pressing them, and “the Israelite foremen, whom Pharaoh’s taskmasters had set over the people, were beaten” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Egypt built its temples and tombs in stone. But houses, palaces, storehouses and fortress walls were built of mud brick: Nile mud mixed with chopped straw, pressed into wooden molds, and dried in the sun. The straw helped bind the clay so the bricks would hold together. Egyptian records from this period list brick quotas for work gangs, so a daily count of bricks fits what is known of how such work was run.

Now the straw stops, but the count stays the same. People must scatter across the countryside to scrape up stubble, the stalks left in the fields after harvest, and still make the full number.

Notice the chain of command. Egyptian taskmasters stand over the workers. Under them are Israelite foremen, chosen from the slaves themselves, who keep the count and answer for any shortfall. Theirs is the cruelest place: answerable to Pharaoh for the numbers, trusted by no one, and beaten when the count is short.

Two messages collide in this chapter. Moses began, ‘This is what the LORD says’. Now the taskmasters announce, ‘This is what Pharaoh says’. The rest of the story will show which king's word stands.

Pharaoh's purpose is plain: ‘Make the work harder ... so they will be occupied and pay no attention’. Work is made so heavy that no one has breath left to think about their God.
passages.later:
Israel's law later remembered this cruelty and forbade it: no Israelite was to “rule over them harshly” (Leviticus 25:43). God's rest for the worker, the Sabbath, was grounded in the memory of slavery: “Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 5:15).

Jesus speaks as the opposite kind of master: “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). Exodus does not predict those words, but it shows the kind of master Jesus is not.
passages.asks: Pharaoh kept people so busy that they had no breath left to think of God. Ask whether anything in your life is working that way: a job, a phone, a schedule. And ask how you might make room, this week, to remember the God who gives rest.

passages.happening:
The Israelite foremen go to Pharaoh: “Why are you treating your servants this way? No straw has been given to your servants, yet we are told, ‘Make bricks!’ Look, your servants are being beaten” (verses 15-16).

“‘You are slackers!’ Pharaoh replied. ‘Slackers! That is why you keep saying, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD.’ Now get to work’” (verses 17-18).

Leaving Pharaoh, they meet Moses and Aaron. “May the LORD look upon you and judge you,” they say, “for you have made us a stench before Pharaoh and his officials; you have placed in their hand a sword to kill us!” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The foremen try the proper way first. They go to Pharaoh himself and appeal to him as his servants. Pharaoh only repeats his charge: lazy, lazy. To a system that measures people by what they produce, wanting to worship looks like idleness.

Then the foremen turn on Moses and Aaron. ‘You have made us a stench’ is a Hebrew way of saying that someone has been made hateful to others. Jacob used the same picture when he complained that his sons had made him ‘a stench to the Canaanites’ (Genesis 34:30). They go further: you have put a sword in Pharaoh's hand. In a land where the king's favor meant life, being made hateful to him was a death sentence waiting to happen.

It is easy to understand them. They are the ones being beaten. Moses came to rescue them, and so far he has only made things worse.

This is the first time Moses' own people turn against him. It will not be the last. And the chapter teaches something the rest of the Bible says again: the first result of obeying God can be more suffering, not less.
passages.later:
Stephen sees a pattern in Moses' life: the one his people rejected was the one God sent (Acts 7:35). John writes of Jesus, “He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him” (John 1:11).

The same Hebrew word for these Israelite officials later names the officers who helped Moses lead the people: “Bring Me seventy of the elders of Israel known to you as leaders and officers of the people” (Numbers 11:16).
passages.asks: The foremen blamed the man God had sent, because things got worse before they got better. Ask whether you have ever blamed God, or his servants, when obedience brought trouble. And ask what it would look like to hold on through a season when doing right seems to make everything harder.

passages.happening: “So Moses returned to the LORD and asked, ‘Lord, why have You brought trouble upon this people? Is this why You sent me? Ever since I went to Pharaoh to speak in Your name, he has brought trouble on this people, and You have not delivered Your people in any way’” (verses 22-23).
passages.hearers:
Moses does not hide his complaint. He takes it straight to God. ‘Why?’ and ‘Is this why You sent me?’ are not polite. They are honest.

This is the shape of many psalms of lament, prayers that cry out to God in pain and ask why. The Bible does not treat such prayers as a lack of faith. It keeps them. A person who complains to God is still talking to God.

Notice too that Moses calls them ‘Your people’. Even in his frustration he holds God to his own words. God said, ‘My people’. Moses throws it back: then why have you not saved them?

The chapter ends with no answer. The next chapter begins with God's reply.
passages.later:
The psalms pray this way. “How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever? How long will You hide Your face from me?” (Psalm 13:1). “Why do You hide Your face and forget our affliction and oppression?” (Psalm 44:24).

God's answer in the next chapter begins, “Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh” (Exodus 6:1).
passages.asks: Moses brought his hardest question straight to God. Ask whether there is a ‘why?’ you have been carrying but not praying. And ask what it would mean to trust that God can hear your honest complaint, as he heard Moses'.
